title: The first American to walk in space didn’t want to come back in

cover.alt: Colour film still: an astronaut in a white suit floats beside the open hatch of a spacecraft, with the blue Earth and white clouds filling the background.

body: On 3 June 1965, less than three months after Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, Ed White opened the hatch of **Gemini 4** and floated out on a tether. He steered with a hand-held gun that squirted pressurised oxygen, and used up its gas sooner than he would have liked. He stayed out about 23 minutes, almost ten minutes longer than planned, until Mission Control radioed “Gemini 4, get back in!” and his commander, Jim McDivitt, coaxed him inside.

slides.alt: Colour film shot from the spacecraft: an astronaut in a white suit drifts slowly away from the craft on a gold-coloured tether, against the blue Earth and swirling clouds.
slides.caption: Gemini 4, 3 June 1965, filmed from the spacecraft: Ed White drifts out on his gold-coloured tether, with Earth’s clouds and ocean far below.

slides.text: It’s the saddest moment of my life.
slides.attribution: Ed White, on being called back inside Gemini 4

slides.heading: 48 minutes with the hatch open
slides.note: Hatch opened at 19:34 UTC and closed at 20:22 UTC. The spacewalk itself lasted about 23 minutes.

slides.prompt: White had no jetpack. What did he use to move himself around outside?
slides.answer: A hand-held gun that squirted oxygen
slides.detail: With the Hand-Held Maneuvering Unit he went about 4.6 m out from the spacecraft and found turning easy to control, but its oxygen ran out sooner than he would have liked.

slides.question: What made getting back inside so slow?
slides.explanation: A spring in the hatch mechanism had failed to compress. His commander, Jim McDivitt, had already helped open it, and it took about 20 minutes after White got in to close it again.
